# APIs {background-color="#0C234B"}

## A URL that returns data

You already know how to read a CSV someone sent you. An **API** is a URL you can
construct that hands back the data directly:

```
https://waterservices.usgs.gov/nwis/dv/?sites=09484000&format=json
```

::: {.fragment}
Three things that buys you:

- **it is current** — no waiting for someone to re-export
- **it is reproducible** — the request is in your code, not in your downloads folder
- **it scales** — one site or four hundred, same three lines
:::

## Why use a wrapper

You could build those URLs yourself. `dataretrieval` builds them for you, and
more importantly parses what comes back into a DataFrame.

```python
import dataretrieval.nwis as nwis

df = nwis.get_record(sites="09484000", service="dv",
                     start="2005-01-01", end="2024-12-31")
```

::: {.fragment}
7,305 rows of daily discharge, indexed by date, in one call.
:::

## The library moved {.smaller}

::: {.fragment}
Every tutorial you will find uses `dataretrieval.nwis`. As of version 1.2.0:

| Old | Status |
|---|---|
| `nwis.get_record()` | deprecated, still works |
| `nwis.get_gwlevels()` | **gone** — raises `NameError` |
| `nwis.get_info()` | still fine |
| — | new: `dataretrieval.waterdata.*` |
:::

::: {.fragment .due-notice}
This is not a trap I set. It is what using other people's code is like, and the
skill is **noticing that the tutorial is older than your library** — usually
because the error message names a function that doesn't exist.
:::

## Reading a deprecation warning

```
DeprecationWarning: `nwis.get_record` is deprecated and will be removed
from `dataretrieval` on or after 2027-05-06; use the appropriate
`waterdata.get_*()` for the service you need instead.
```

::: {.incremental}
- It tells you **what** is going away
- It tells you **when**
- It tells you **what to use instead**
:::

::: {.fragment}
A warning is not an error. Your code still runs. But a warning you ignore for
two years becomes an error on a deadline.
:::

## Your turn: which function?

You need **groundwater levels** for a list of well IDs. `nwis.get_gwlevels` is
gone. Pick the replacement.

```{pyodide}
    "waterdata.get_daily": "daily summary values from a continuous sensor",
    "waterdata.get_continuous": "15-minute sensor readings",
    "waterdata.get_field_measurements": "discrete readings taken by hand in the field",
    "waterdata.get_samples": "laboratory water-quality analyses",

```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_api
choice = ______
print(f"{choice}: {descriptions[choice]}")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_api"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Most water-level readings in a basin monitoring network are made by somebody
driving out with a steel tape a few times a year — not by a logger.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_api"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
choice = "waterdata.get_field_measurements"
```

Discrete, manual readings. `get_continuous` and `get_daily` would return
almost nothing — very few wells in the Tucson basin are instrumented, and the
ones that are have short records.

Choosing the wrong one here doesn't error. It returns an empty DataFrame, and
you spend twenty minutes wondering why the basin has no data.
:::
:::

# Not depending on uptime {background-color="#AB0520"}

## The problem, concretely

Twelve people. One room. One API. One class period.

::: {.incremental}
- NWIS rate-limits by IP, and the whole room shares one
- The samples endpoint times out on large queries even when it's healthy
- Conference wifi exists
:::

::: {.fragment .due-notice}
**A lab that depends on someone else's uptime is a lab that fails in class.**
Every notebook in this course that touches an API ships a cached copy.
:::

## The pattern

```python
def load_sabino():
    """Daily discharge at Sabino Creek. Live if possible, cached if not."""
    try:
        df = nwis.get_record(sites=SABINO, service="dv", ...)
        print(f"live from NWIS: {len(df):,} rows")
        return tidy(df)
    except Exception as exc:
        print(f"live fetch failed ({type(exc).__name__}); using the cached copy")
        return pd.read_csv(DATA / "cache" / f"nwis_{SABINO}_dv.csv",
                           parse_dates=["datetime"])
```

::: {.fragment}
Three properties worth copying: both paths return **the same columns**, the
function **says which one ran**, and the failure is **not silent**.
:::

## Your turn: complete the fallback

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_fallback
def fetch_live(site):
    raise ConnectionError("NWIS is not answering")   # pretend the API is down

def read_cache(site):
    return f"cached data for {site}"
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_fallback
def load(site):
    try:
        return ______
    except Exception as exc:
        print(f"live fetch failed ({type(exc).__name__}); using cache")
        return ______

load("09484000")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_fallback"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Try the live one first. If anything at all goes wrong, fall back to the cache.
Both branches have to `return`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_fallback"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
try:
    return fetch_live(site)
except Exception as exc:
    print(...)
    return read_cache(site)
```

Catching bare `Exception` is usually bad practice — it hides bugs in your own
code. Here it is right, because **every** failure mode should end the same way:
you cannot enumerate all the ways a network call can fail, and the student needs
the lab to keep going regardless.
:::
:::

## Where the cache comes from

Committed data with no provenance rots into magic numbers nobody dares change.
So the cache is *generated*:

```bash
python scripts/fetch_data.py --list    # what gets built
python scripts/fetch_data.py           # rebuild it
```

::: {.fragment}
Every dataset in `data/` came from that script, and the script is in the repo.
If you want to know where a number came from, you can read it.
:::

::: {.fragment}
The rule for size: **over about 10 MB, fetch it with a hash instead of
committing it.** Nothing in this course is close, but your thesis will be.
:::

# What actually arrives {background-color="#0C234B"}

## Column names are not for you

```
['00060_Mean', '00060_Mean_cd', 'site_no']
```

::: {.fragment}
`00060` is the USGS parameter code for discharge in cubic feet per second.
`_cd` is the qualifier column — `A` for approved, `P` for provisional.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Rename on the way in.** Every line you write afterward reads better, and you
only have to look up the parameter code once.

```python
df = df.rename(columns={"00060_Mean": "discharge_cfs"})
```
:::

## Your turn: rename on the way in

Give these columns names a human can read.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_rename
import pandas as pd
raw = pd.DataFrame({
    "00060_Mean": [64.2, 55.3, 220.0],
    "00060_Mean_cd": ["A", "A", "P"],
    "site_no": ["09484000"] * 3,
})
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_rename
tidy = raw.rename(columns=______)
print(list(tidy.columns))
tidy
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_rename"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

`.rename(columns=...)` takes a dictionary mapping old name to new. You only have
to list the ones you're changing.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_rename"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
tidy = raw.rename(columns={
    "00060_Mean": "discharge_cfs",
    "00060_Mean_cd": "qualifier",
})
```

Note the unit is in the name. `discharge` alone invites somebody to assume m³/s
six months from now, and the conversion factor between them is 35.3 — big enough
that the mistake shows up, small enough that it might not.
:::
:::

## Provisional means provisional

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| min-lines: 6
qualifiers = {"A": 3908, "A, e": 512, "P": 216}

for code, n in qualifiers.items():
    meaning = {"A": "approved", "A, e": "approved, estimated",
               "P": "provisional — may change"}[code]
    print(f"{code:6s} {n:5d}  {meaning}")
```

::: {.fragment}
Recent data is provisional and **will** be revised. If your figure needs to be
reproducible, record the date you pulled it — or better, pin to a cached copy
and say so.
:::
